extracted.intended_audience: communication and media researchers; social scientists; graduate students in media studies
extracted.subtask_description: An empirical study of how recipients (readers) select newspaper and magazine articles, testing whether news factors or formal article characteristics drive media use; uses content analysis and audience diary data with bivariate and multivariate analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: News factors as selection criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: News factors (news value) function as selection criteria for recipients; they indicate relevance and can be used to reduce complexity when choosing what to read.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper treats news factors as plausible human information-processing criteria; cognitive psychology (attention) offers explanations for their effectiveness. Bivariate analyses in the study show that news factors influence media use: respondents prefer articles of high news value to those of lower news value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevance as central determinant
rubrics_metrics.description: Perceived relevance is the central mechanism by which news factors influence selection: news factors signal relevance to readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The argument is that readers use cues (news factors) to judge relevance efficiently. The discussion raises the question whether readers instead rely on formal characteristics as proxies for relevance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal article characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Formal characteristics of an article (e.g., presentation, structure, typographic or formal features) determine selection more strongly than news factors in multivariate analyses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multivariate results in the study qualify bivariate findings: not so much the news factors but rather the formal contribution characteristics determine article selection. The paper discusses that recipients might use these formal features as shortcuts to judge relevance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shared human information-processing assumption
rubrics_metrics.description: Assumes journalists and recipients select information according to the same general human principles of information processing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This assumption underpins the transfer of news-value concepts from studies of journalistic selection to studies of audience selection; cognitive-psychological theories (especially attention) are invoked to justify it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of cognitive/attention psychology as explanatory framework
rubrics_metrics.description: The psychology of attention is used to explain why news factors serve as effective selection criteria.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attention research suggests mechanisms for why certain features stand out and are chosen; this theoretical framing justifies analyzing news factors as indicators of relevance and efficiency in complexity reduction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical method: content analysis + audience diaries
rubrics_metrics.description: Combine content analysis of media contributions with media-use data derived from audience diaries (one-week paper and magazine use) to study selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The approach compares characteristics of articles that were read vs. not read. This combined-method design is presented as appropriate to link article-level features to individual-level reading behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analytical strategy: bivariate vs multivariate analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Bivariate analyses of news factors in read vs unread articles indicate influence of news factors; multivariate analyses may reveal different primary predictors (e.g., formal characteristics).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The study demonstrates the need to move beyond bivariate comparisons because controlling for multiple variables can change which predictors appear most important; use multivariate models to test whether news factors independently predict selection once formal features and other covariates are included.
